title: Accelerated Gradient Methods for Nonconvex Optimization: Escape Trajectories From Strict Saddle Points and Convergence to Local Minima
summary: This paper considers the problem of understanding the behavior of a general class of accelerated gradient methods on smooth nonconvex functions. Motivated by some recent works that have proposed effective algorithms, based on Polyak's heavy ball method and the Nesterov accelerated gradient method, to achieve convergence to a local minimum of nonconvex functions, this work proposes a broad class of Nesterov-type accelerated methods and puts forth a rigorous study of these methods encompassing the escape from saddle points and convergence to local minima through both an asymptotic and a non-asymptotic analysis. In the asymptotic regime, this paper answers an open question of whether Nesterov's accelerated gradient method (NAG) with variable momentum parameter avoids strict saddle points almost surely. This work also develops two metrics of asymptotic rates of convergence and divergence, and evaluates these two metrics for several popular standard accelerated methods such as the NAG and Nesterov's accelerated gradient with constant momentum (NCM) near strict saddle points. In the non-asymptotic regime, this work provides an analysis that leads to the "linear" exit time estimates from strict saddle neighborhoods for trajectories of these accelerated methods as well the necessary conditions for the existence of such trajectories. Finally, this work studies a sub-class of accelerated methods that can converge in convex neighborhoods of nonconvex functions with a near optimal rate to a local minimum and at the same time this sub-class offers superior saddle-escape behavior compared to that of NAG.
core_methodology: The paper presents a rigorous study of Nesterov-type accelerated gradient methods for nonconvex optimization, focusing on their behavior near saddle points and convergence to local minima. It includes both asymptotic and non-asymptotic analyses, with specific attention to escape trajectories from strict saddle points and convergence conditions.
data_sources: Not explicitly mentioned in the abstract, but typically applies to any numerical optimization problem, potentially including financial model calibration or machine learning loss surfaces.
alpha_potential: Potential applications in optimizing complex trading strategies or portfolio construction problems where the objective function is nonconvex and may contain saddle points. Particularly relevant for high-dimensional optimization problems in quant finance.

title: Deep conditional distribution learning via conditional F\"ollmer flow
summary: We introduce an ordinary differential equation (ODE) based deep generative method for learning conditional distributions, named Conditional F\"ollmer Flow. Starting from a standard Gaussian distribution, the proposed flow could approximate the target conditional distribution very well when the time is close to 1. For effective implementation, we discretize the flow with Euler's method where we estimate the velocity field nonparametrically using a deep neural network. Furthermore, we also establish the convergence result for the Wasserstein-2 distance between the distribution of the learned samples and the target conditional distribution, providing the first comprehensive end-to-end error analysis for conditional distribution learning via ODE flow. Our numerical experiments showcase its effectiveness across a range of scenarios, from standard nonparametric conditional density estimation problems to more intricate challenges involving image data, illustrating its superiority over various existing conditional density estimation methods.
core_methodology: The paper introduces an ODE-based deep generative method for learning conditional distributions, named Conditional Föllmer Flow. It starts from a standard Gaussian distribution and approximates the target conditional distribution by discretizing the flow with Euler's method and estimating the velocity field using a deep neural network.
data_sources: The paper mentions numerical experiments on standard nonparametric conditional density estimation problems and image data, but does not specify financial data sources.
alpha_potential: The methodology could be adapted for predicting conditional distributions in financial markets, such as forecasting asset returns based on conditioning variables, which could be valuable for portfolio optimization and risk management.

title: Reinforcement Learning in MDPs with Information-Ordered Policies
summary: Many operational Markov decision processes provide structured information where a trajectory generated under one policy may also reveal how other policies would have performed. We formalize this through an information order over a parameterized policy class, writing $\pi_{\theta'} \preceq \pi_\theta$ when data collected under $\pi_\theta$ can be used to estimate the long-run average cost of $\pi_{\theta'}$. We develop an epoch-based reinforcement learning algorithm for infinite-horizon average-cost MDPs with continuous state and action spaces that exploits this order through counterfactual inference. For a $d$-dimensional policy class whose information order has width $w$, the algorithm achieves $\widetilde O(H\sqrt{wdT/\alpha})$ regret relative to the optimal policy in the class, where $H$ is a bias span upper bound and $\alpha$ denotes an "information ratio". Thus, the width captures the effective exploration complexity of the problem, interpolating between full counterfactual feedback and unstructured policy learning. We instantiate the framework in lost-sales inventory systems with positive lead times, dual-sourcing systems governed by dual-index policies, and queues with state-dependent service rates. These applications yield new regret guarantees without requiring global convexity of the average-cost function or specialized arrival-rate structure. Numerical experiments show that exploiting the information order substantially improves learning performance over existing general-purpose and problem-specific benchmarks.
core_methodology: Reinforcement learning algorithm for infinite-horizon average-cost MDPs with continuous state and action spaces that exploits an information order over a parameterized policy class for counterfactual inference.
data_sources: Simulated or operational data from systems like lost-sales inventory systems, dual-sourcing systems, and queues with state-dependent service rates.
alpha_potential: Potential to optimize trading strategies by better understanding policy performance through structured information and counterfactual inference, particularly in systems with continuous state and action spaces.

title: Structural Causal Bottleneck Models
summary: We introduce structural causal bottleneck models (SCBMs), a novel class of structural causal models in which causal effects between high-dimensional variables are mediated by low-dimensional summary statistics, or *bottlenecks*. SCBMs provide a flexible framework for mechanism-specific, target-dependent dimension reduction while remaining estimable via standard learning algorithms. We prove that bottleneck variables are identifiable up to bijection from observational data, and validate this experimentally. We then study causal effect estimation in linear SCBMs under three standard adjustment strategies. For instrumental variables, we identify a population-level non-identifiability of na\"ive two-stage least squares when all variables are high-dimensional, and show that bottleneck representations restore identification. For mediation and backdoor adjustment, we prove that conditioning on bottleneck variables yields valid effect estimates with explicit finite-sample efficiency gains over conditioning on full high-dimensional variables. We argue that SCBMs provide a principled alternative to existing causal dimension reduction frameworks such as causal representation learning and causal abstractions.
core_methodology: Structural causal models with low-dimensional bottleneck variables that mediate high-dimensional causal relationships
data_sources: Theoretical framework applicable to any high-dimensional financial data (market prices, order book data, alternative data)
alpha_potential: Potential to identify more robust causal relationships in market data by focusing on key bottleneck variables, possibly leading to higher quality alpha signals with better generalization

title: Dynamics of Stochastic Momentum with Sparse Updates in High Dimensions
summary: Existing theory of momentum assumes that gradients arrive at every parameter at a roughly constant rate, an assumption violated in practice by heavy-tailed data distributions and modern architectures. We theoretically analyze the dynamics of two tractable models of momentum under sparse updates: a least squares model with sparse inputs and a logistic regression model with a rare class. Both admit exact closed-form second-moment dynamics whose high-dimensional limits we characterize across three scaling exponents for sparsity, batch size, and momentum decay. The phase structure on both problems is governed by the ratio of two intrinsic timescales: a momentum retention timescale (how many active updates the buffer survives) and a learning timescale (how many active updates it takes to reduce the squared error). When learning is much slower than retention, the limit matches SGD; when learning is faster, the system is unstable; where the timescales coincide, we recover classical heavy-ball dynamics. The oscillatory dynamics occur at different momentum values for different token sparsity, creating a spectral conflict for global momentum across token frequencies.
core_methodology: Theoretical analysis of momentum dynamics under sparse updates in high dimensions, focusing on least squares and logistic regression models with rare classes.
data_sources: Not explicitly mentioned, but likely involves synthetic or simulated datasets to study sparse updates and heavy-tailed distributions.
alpha_potential: Potential insights into improving momentum-based trading strategies by accounting for sparse updates and varying token sparsity, which could lead to better adaptation to market conditions.

title: Online Inference for Quantile Distributional Reinforcement Learning
summary: In this paper, we study online statistical inference for quantile-based distributional policy evaluation, which aims to characterize the distribution of discounted cumulative rewards under a given policy. To obtain a finite-dimensional representation of the return distribution, we consider the fixed point $\bm\eta_m$ of the quantile-projected distributional Bellman equation, parameterized by the quantile vector $\bm\theta_m$. We develop two online inference procedures for $\bm\theta_m$, covering synchronous and asynchronous sampling from a generative model as well as Markovian data. The first method uses the trajectory of quantile temporal-difference learning (QTD). We establish functional central limit theorems for the partial sums of QTD iterates and construct a recursively computable random-scaling statistic. The resulting confidence intervals have asymptotically exact coverage at deterministic horizons, with length of order $T^{-1/2}$ in probability. The second method constructs anytime-valid confidence intervals directly from samples. Exploiting the monotonicity of the quantile Bellman map, we develop a computationally explicit coordinate-shaving algorithm with finite-sample simultaneous coverage. Under positive limiting state-visit frequencies, the resulting confidence intervals have lengths of order $\sqrt{\log\log T/T}$, which we establish as classwise optimal through a matching lower bound. Together, these results provide complementary guarantees for online inference in quantile distributional reinforcement learning, combining asymptotically exact fixed-horizon inference with finite-sample anytime validity.
core_methodology: Quantile-based distributional reinforcement learning with online inference for policy evaluation, using quantile temporal-difference learning and a coordinate-shaving algorithm for confidence interval construction.
data_sources: Generative model samples or Markovian data (theoretical framework applicable to financial time series data).
alpha_potential: Potential for improving risk-aware decision-making in trading by better characterizing the distribution of returns and managing tail risks, though direct trading applications would require adaptation to market data.

title: Online Inference in Distributional Temporal-Difference Learning
summary: We study online statistical inference for functionals of the return distribution under a fixed policy. The return distribution is estimated by nonparametric distributional temporal-difference learning from a single Markov trajectory. For the Polyak--Ruppert averaged estimator, we prove that its root-$T$ error converges weakly to a centered Gaussian random element in Cram\'er space. We also prove that, conditionally on the observed trajectory, the root-$T$ difference between the bootstrap and original averages converges weakly to the same Gaussian limit. These results justify bootstrap inference for smooth statistical functionals, including variance, CVaR, expected shortfall, and expectiles. For nonsmooth statistical functionals, we develop a local asymptotic theory for the estimated return CDF over $T^{-1/2}$-neighborhoods of finitely many thresholds, together with its bootstrap analogue. This theory allows us to conduct inference for nonsmooth statistical functionals characterized by CDF equations, including return quantiles.
core_methodology: Nonparametric distributional temporal-difference learning for estimating return distributions from Markov trajectories, with bootstrap inference for both smooth and nonsmooth statistical functionals.
data_sources: Single Markov trajectory (can be interpreted as financial time series data representing state transitions in market conditions).
alpha_potential: Provides statistically robust methods for estimating risk measures (CVaR, expected shortfall, quantiles) which can enhance risk-managed trading strategies and portfolio optimization.

title: CVaR anchor regression protects against rare shifts
summary: We study prediction in new environments when the training data contains rare, large distribution shifts. Anchor regression penalizes the average of the squared mean residual across environments. It protects against shifts in an ellipsoid determined by the second moment of the training shifts. Covering rare shifts may therefore require a large penalty $\gamma \gg 1$, expanding the ellipsoid in every direction and reducing accuracy on common environments. We propose CVaR anchor regression, which replaces the average of the squared mean residuals with a tail average. We prove an exact worst-case risk guarantee under a linear structural model that allows for heteroscedastic noise. CVaR anchor regression protects against shifts in a union of ellipsoids determined by second moments of the shifts in the worst $\alpha$-fraction of environments. For $\alpha$ small enough, this is the scaled convex hull of the training shifts and their negatives. It therefore covers all training shifts when $\gamma \geq 1$. Unlike CVaR or GroupDRO applied directly to prediction risks, CVaR anchor regression does not give environments more weight solely because their noise levels are high. Examples show how the method can improve protection against rare shifts while retaining accuracy on common environments. We illustrate the method on the New York City taxi dataset.
core_methodology: CVaR anchor regression, which focuses on improving prediction robustness in environments with rare, large distribution shifts by using a tail-average approach instead of mean squared residuals.
data_sources: New York City taxi dataset (mentioned), but method is generalizable to financial time-series data with regime shifts.
alpha_potential: Potential to improve robustness of trading strategies during rare but impactful market regime shifts (e.g., flash crashes, monetary policy surprises). Offers better trade-off between protection against tail events and performance in normal regimes compared to standard robust regression methods.

title: Sharp Asymptotic Theory of Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Gaussian Processes with an RBF Kernel
summary: Gaussian processes (GPs) are widely used across machine learning, spatial statistics, time-series analysis, optimization, Bayesian statistics, and scientific applications. A central component of a GP model is its kernel, which is typically specified through a parametric family. Among the most widely used choices is the radial basis function (RBF), also known as the squared exponential or Gaussian kernel, owing to its simple form, smoothness, and flexibility. In practice, the kernel parameters are routinely estimated by the maximum likelihood estimators (MLEs), as implemented by standard GP software. Despite this widespread use, the asymptotic behavior of the MLEs remains poorly understood under fixed-domain asymptotics, even for the RBF kernel. The main difficulty arises from the increasingly strong dependence among densely sampled observations and the nonlinear dependence of the covariance matrix on the kernel parameters. In this paper, we address this gap by providing, to the best of our knowledge, the first complete asymptotic characterization of the joint MLE of the spatial variance, lengthscale, and nugget variance under fixed-domain asymptotics. We establish consistency, derive convergence rates for all three parameters, prove joint asymptotic normality, and show that these rates are minimax optimal.
core_methodology: Asymptotic analysis of maximum likelihood estimators (MLEs) for Gaussian processes (GPs) with RBF kernels, focusing on consistency, convergence rates, and asymptotic normality under fixed-domain asymptotics.
data_sources: Theoretical study based on Gaussian process models, applicable to any financial time series or spatial data where GPs are used for modeling.
alpha_potential: Provides theoretical foundation for improving parameter estimation in GP models used for financial forecasting, volatility modeling, or other time series analyses. Could enhance predictive models by ensuring more accurate kernel parameter estimation.
